name: St. Mary's Basilica
label: St. Mary's Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rynek Główny' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rynek Główny' (way/201133718): middle (416 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26195267: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Mary's Basilica' (97 m across).
notes: Gothic church with two uneven towers and a famous altarpiece.

text.description:
St. Mary's Basilica is the Gothic brick church that rises over the northeastern corner of Kraków's Main Market Square. The basilica stands about 80 m tall, and its two towers differ in height. The church dates from the 14th century, though its foundations go back to the early 13th. It is also known for its carved wooden altarpiece by Veit Stoss, which is inside. Every hour a trumpet call, the Hejnał mariacki, sounds from the taller tower and stops mid-tune. That makes a nice moment to film a short clip of the square.

The basilica photographs best from out in the square, where you can step back far enough to fit the towers in. The classic frame takes in the church and the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) together, with the brick walls, steep roofs and the two towers set against the sky. For a different view, look through the arches of the Cloth Hall and let them frame the tower in the gap. Or walk to Mały Rynek, the smaller square beside the main one, for a quieter angle.

If the facade looks partly covered, that may be building work, as towers were reported under repair in summer 2025. Take a few frames from different spots in case scaffolding gets in the way.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Kraków, at Mariacki Square on the northeastern corner of the Main Market Square (Rynek Główny), close to ul. Floriańska.
text.directions_text: There are no tram or rail stops right at this spot, so start from the Old Town and the Main Market Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the basilica and the Cloth Hall into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the church. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower tops and the gilded crown.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rynek Główny (northeastern corner, near ul. Floriańska). The basilica and the Cloth Hall together in one frame, the classic postcard composition of the Main Market Square. The northeastern corner near ul. Floriańska is a separate, closer viewpoint that shows the basilica and the Cloth Hall together in one frame. This is the classic postcard view of the Main Market Square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with a vertical grid line so they stand straight. Keep the phone level, since tilting it makes the towers lean. Leave a little sky above the taller tower. For a second shot, frame the tower through the Cloth Hall arches, or try Mały Rynek for a quieter angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brick facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo or a short video around the hour to catch the trumpet call.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is nearly empty and the basilica is lit from the east.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the basilica is a working church and interior photography needs a photo permit, so check the official site before you go.

name: Wawel Castle
label: Wawel Castle
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/785550415: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Zamek Wawel' (454 m across).
notes: Former royal residence on a hill above the Vistula.

text.description: Wawel Castle is the old royal residence of Poland, standing on a limestone hill above the left bank of the Vistula in Kraków. It was begun on the orders of King Casimir III the Great, and the current castle dates from the 14th century. It was then added to over many generations, so the buildings gather around a Renaissance courtyard and show a mix of medieval, Renaissance and Baroque styles. Wawel Cathedral, where Polish monarchs were crowned and buried, stands right beside it. In 1978 the hill became part of Kraków's Historic Centre, the first place on the World Heritage list. It photographs well because the pale walls, towers and rooftops sit on a raised hill, so the whole group reads as one skyline. Start with a wide shot to show the castle against the sky, then move in for details such as roof edges, windows and towers. Keep the phone level, using the gridlines, because tall walls look as if they lean when the phone is tilted up. If you want a fun extra, a modern fire-breathing dragon statue stands on the lower slopes by the river, in front of the Dragon's Den cave.
text.geographic_location: Wawel Hill, on the left bank of the Vistula in Kraków, next to Wawel Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Head for Wawel Hill beside the Vistula from Kraków's Old Town and aim for the foot of the hill. Keep the hill and its walls ahead of you as you go. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m north-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the main view of the castle. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close and want walls and towers in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roofs, turrets and other details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Face that direction so the walls and rooflines fill the frame, and step a few paces back if the top is cut off.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the main tower or roofline up with a horizontal line so the buildings look straight. Leave some sky above the roofs to show the hill's height. For a second picture, go in tight with the telephoto on a detail such as a roof edge or window.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stonework and sky keep their detail. If the castle won't fit in the frame, try panorama, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the walls and fewer people in the shot. In the evening, try night mode, but hold the phone very still.

text.access_note: Parts of the castle and its exhibitions are likely to need tickets and have visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall walls look as if they lean, which gridlines help to avoid.
Parts of the castle and its exhibitions are likely to be ticketed or have visiting rules.

name: Oskar Schindler's Enamel Factory
label: Schindler's Factory
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ulica Lipowa' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of ulica Lipowa nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/136648568: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Oskar Schindler's Enamel Factory' (84 m across).
notes: Factory-turned-museum about Kraków during the Nazi occupation.

text.description:
This is the former enamel factory at Lipowa 4 in Zabłocie, made widely known by the 1993 film Schindler's List. The building you see from the street is the old administration block. Today the site holds two museums: a branch of the Historical Museum of the City of Kraków, and the Museum of Contemporary Art in Kraków in the former workshops. Oskar Schindler took over the factory in 1939 and renamed it Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik in January 1940. The number of Jewish workers grew from just over 150 in 1940 to around 1,100 by 1944. The city museum's exhibition on Kraków under occupation has been here since 2007. The tour includes the desk and stairs from the film set.

It photographs well because the front is plain and honest, and it still looks much as it did in the 1940s. From the street you can take in the renovated facade, the entrance gate and the area where visitors queue, all in one frame. That is enough for a strong, quiet picture without going inside. Keep the mood in mind: this is a serious place, and a straight, uncluttered shot suits it better than a clever angle.

Stand on the street side, opposite the front of number 4, and keep the whole width of the facade in view. Hold the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. If people are queuing at the gate, wait a moment for a gap, or include them for a sense of scale, but be considerate of anyone who might be recognisable.
text.geographic_location: In the Zabłocie district of Kraków, at ulica Lipowa 4. The Museum of Contemporary Art in Kraków is on the same site, in the former workshops.
text.directions_text: Type 'Lipowa 4, Kraków' into your map app to find the spot in the Zabłocie district. Once on the street, look for the building with the entrance gate and the museum queue area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives the most natural-looking facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is too narrow to fit the whole front in, and keep the building centred so the edges do not stretch. Skip the telephoto unless you want a close detail of the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on ulica Lipowa (opposite the Lipowa 4 front facade, on the street side). The renovated front of the former enamel factory administration building at Lipowa 4, with the entrance gate and the museum's queue area in the frame. Opposite the Lipowa 4 front facade, on the street side. You will see the renovated front of the former administration building, with the entrance gate and the museum's queue area in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so it does not lean. Put the gate in the centre or on a third, and leave a little street in the foreground so the building has room. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a tighter one of the gate. Avoid pointing the phone upwards, which makes the walls tilt.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a touch if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail. Do not use portrait mode on the building; it works best for people. Keep the phone steady against your body or a wall for a sharp shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is best for reading the facade clearly. Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter at the gate, but check how the light falls on the front when you arrive.

text.access_note: The facade and gate can be seen from the street without a ticket, but the museum inside is a ticketed site and the courtyard is not open public space, so check the official site before you go for tickets, opening times and photo rules.

name: Planty Park
label: Planty Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brama Floriańska' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Brama Floriańska' (way/39357538): middle (16 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1221128266: large area 'Planty Park in Krakow' (1622 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Green ring of parks around the Old Town.

text.description:
Planty is the green ring that wraps around Krakow's Old Town, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to take relaxed, leafy photos. It was laid out between 1822 and 1830 on the line of the medieval defensive walls, which had been pulled down. The park covers about 21 hectares and runs for roughly 4 km as a chain of thirty smaller gardens, with statues, monuments and fountains along the way. Two pieces of the old defences were kept: the Florian Gate and the Barbican beside it. The Barbican is one of only three fortified outposts of its kind still standing in Europe.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is the Florian Gate (Brama Floriańska) seen from the Planty walk just outside it, looking back along the park. The tree-lined paths frame the gate, and the greenery softens the stonework. The main loop passes the Barbican too, so you can take both pictures in one short stroll. Because Planty is a long ring, you do not need to walk it all. Pick one or two spots, wait for a gap in the walkers, and shoot along the paths so the lines lead the eye to the gate. Flowers, autumn colour and fog change the look through the year. For a calmer alternative to the gate, try the Bernatka footbridge, where trees and path lines lead away from you.
text.geographic_location: Planty Park encircles the Old Town of Krakow, on the line of the former city walls. The Florian Gate viewpoint is on its northern side, beside the Barbican, where the Royal Road leaves the Old Town towards Kleparz.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, train or tram stop at this spot, so start from the Old Town and walk to the Florian Gate on its northern edge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and the tree-lined paths. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the leafy arch overhead. A telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the gate's details from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Brama Floriańska (the Planty walk just outside the gate, looking back along the park). The Florian Gate framed by the tree-lined Planty paths and the park's greenery. From here the gate sits framed by the tree-lined paths and the park's greenery. Planty Park lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the gate on one of the vertical lines. Let the path run from the bottom of the frame towards the gate, with tree trunks and branches on both sides. For a different view, the Barbican's round brick towers rise above green trees with the pond and paths in the foreground. The Bernatka footbridge gives a quieter view over the Planty greenery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the stone and leaves. Try Live Photos if people are walking through, so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the paths. Seasonal changes such as flowers, autumn colour and fog can make the view more interesting.

text.access_note: Planty is an open public park. The Barbican may be closed at times, but you do not need to go inside for these views.

name: Wawel Dragon
label: Wawel Dragon
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bulwar Czerwieński' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bulwar Czerwieński nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/278057698: the OpenStreetMap point 'Wawel Dragon'.
notes: Fire-breathing dragon statue below Wawel Hill.

text.description: The Wawel Dragon is a bronze statue at the foot of Wawel Hill, beside the Vistula and in front of the cave said to be the dragon's den. It stands for the best-known legend in Krakow: a dragon that terrorised the townspeople until a cobbler named Skuba tricked it into drinking so much river water that it burst. The statue was designed by the sculptor Bronisław Chromy, finished in 1969 and put in its present place in 1972. It is 6 metres tall and sits on a large limestone boulder. What draws the crowds is that it breathes fire. The flame comes on by itself every few minutes, and visitors can also set it off by text message. The timing varies, and the flame is sometimes switched off for maintenance. It photographs well for two reasons. The dragon is a strong, simple shape, and Wawel Hill rises directly behind it. From the riverside walk you can fit the dragon, the western face of the castle and the river into one frame. That is the view this map point is built around. For a close-up of the dragon, go to the statue itself. If you want the whole hill, Most Dębnicki gives a wider scene in which the dragon is only a small part, if it shows at all. The statue is a popular attraction, so keep your phone ready.
text.geographic_location: At the foot of Wawel Hill in Krakow, on the bank of the Vistula, in front of the dragon's den below the castle.
text.directions_text: Head for the foot of Wawel Hill on the river side. The dragon statue is in front of the dragon's den, right below the castle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the dragon, the castle and the river into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a balanced view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dragon's head and flame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bulwar Czerwieński (riverbank walkway below the castle hill; one guide places the best panorama on the boulevard below the Sheraton Hotel). A wider frame with the dragon in the foreground and the western face of Wawel Castle and the Vistula behind it. The riverbank walkway below the castle hill. From here the dragon sits in the foreground, with the western face of Wawel Castle and the Vistula behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dragon on a lower third line, with the castle wall filling the upper part. Keep the horizon level. For a close-up of the flame, the statue itself is the better place. If you want the whole hill, try Most Dębnicki, where the dragon will be small or out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dragon to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the flame does not turn into a white blob. A Live Photo can catch the moment the fire starts. Once the light fades, night mode helps, but hold the phone very still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is established for this spot. If you want the flame in your shot, wait for it to start, but remember it can be switched off for maintenance.

text.access_note: The statue stands in an open public area and is free to see, but the dragon's den cave is a separate ticketed and seasonal visit, so check the official site before you go.

name: Wawel Cathedral
label: Wawel Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bulwar Czerwieński' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bulwar Czerwieński nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/85151350: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Archcathedral Basilica of Saints Stanislaus and Wenceslaus' (93 m across).
notes: Coronation church of Polish kings with the golden Sigismund Chapel dome.

text.description:
Wawel Cathedral sits on Wawel Hill, part of the Wawel Castle complex, and is nearly 1,000 years old. The Gothic building you see today is the third church on this spot. Its consecration was in 1364, and from 1320 until 1764 it was where Polish monarchs were crowned. Over the centuries, rulers added chapels in different styles, so the outside is a mix of Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and later touches. The golden-domed Sigismund's Chapel is the best known of them.

The cathedral photographs best from a distance, with the hill and the water doing some of the work. From here you look across the water at the castle's silhouette, with the bend of the Vistula in view and a reflection beneath it.

Keep the horizon level and let the river fill the lower part of the frame. If you want a second angle, Most Dębnicki shows the hill with the river curving through the foreground. Plac Wielkiej Armii Napoleona is a possible spot for night views of the lit-up castle, but check it on arrival.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is on Wawel Hill in Kraków, within the Wawel Castle complex.
text.directions_text: Bulwar Czerwieński is the riverside boulevard at the foot of Wawel Hill, so check a map on your phone for the route from where you are. The hill itself is not the place for this shot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a low, wide view of the hill, river and reflection. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cathedral and its golden dome from the rest of the castle. Use the default lens (1x) for a balanced, natural view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bulwar Czerwieński (riverside boulevard at the foot of Wawel Hill, facing the castle across the water). The castle's silhouette above the river, with the water reflecting it and the bend of the Vistula in view. From here the cathedral lies to the east, on top of the hill. The riverside gives you the silhouette above the water and the bend of the Vistula.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third so the reflection has room. Keep the hill and its skyline in the upper part of the frame. For a second view, try Most Dębnicki, where the river curves through the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the castle to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the reflection stays clear. As the light fades, use night mode and rest your elbows on the boulevard wall or railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the water reflects the castle and the light is softest.

text.access_note: The riverside boulevard is open public space, but the cathedral is a place of worship and part of the Wawel complex, so check the official site before you go for access and photography rules, especially in the royal tombs and crypts.
claims_not_in_sources: The golden dome of Sigismund's Chapel may be visible from the riverside boulevard, depending on trees and the angle.
Resting your elbows on a wall or railing helps keep a phone steady in low light.
Photography is generally allowed in the cathedral's main part but restricted in the royal tombs and crypts.

name: Main Square, Kraków
label: Main Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rynek Główny' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Rynek Główny and Floriańska (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/201133718: 'Adam Mickiewicz Monument', the best-known feature inside 'Main Square' (418 m across).
notes: The huge medieval market square at the heart of the Old Town.

text.description:
Kraków's Main Square is the great open heart of the Old Town. It dates back to the 13th century, covers about 4 hectares and is often described as one of the largest medieval town squares in Europe. The Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) sits in the middle, rebuilt in the Renaissance style after a fire in 1555, with arcades added in the 19th century. The Gothic towers of St Mary's Basilica rise above the square, and the Adam Mickiewicz Monument of 1898 stands nearby. It was rebuilt after the Second World War, when the original was destroyed. The whole Old Town has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1978.

The square photographs well because everything is on a human scale and the landmarks line up. From the northeast corner, where Floriańska Street meets the square, the basilica and the Cloth Hall fit into one frame. This is the classic postcard composition. The colourful townhouse fronts help to frame it, and the square is large enough that you can step back for a wider view.

A few practical points. The basilica's hourly trumpet call (the hejnal) is hard to photograph from the square, even with zoom, so enjoy it by ear instead. Photography inside the basilica is restricted. Climbing the Town Hall Tower or the basilica tower is a separate, paid visit, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Kraków's Old Town, on the Royal Road between the Barbican to the north and Wawel Castle to the south.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town and walk to the Main Square. Make for the northeast corner of the square, where Floriańska Street meets it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the basilica and the Cloth Hall together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the basilica towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Rynek Główny and Floriańska (northeast corner of the square, where Floriańska Street meets it). St Mary's Basilica and the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) together in one frame, the classic postcard composition. Stand on Rynek Główny, at the northeast corner of the square where Floriańska Street meets it. From here St Mary's Basilica and the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) sit together in one frame, and the Mickiewicz Monument lies to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the Cloth Hall along the lower third, with the basilica towers rising behind it. Keep the phone level so the buildings don't lean. For a second view, stand by the Mickiewicz Monument and shoot past the Cloth Hall arcades towards the basilica, which keeps the café clutter out of the frame. Floriańska Street also makes a good shot, with its colourful townhouse fronts leading towards the basilica towers in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the basilica facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Try a Live Photo if people are crossing the square, then pick the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 7-8 AM, when the light falls well on the basilica facade and the square is quiet.

text.access_note: The square itself is an open public space. The Town Hall Tower and basilica tower are separate, paid visits (the basilica tower is open seasonally), so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: An ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps fit both the basilica and the Cloth Hall into one frame from the corner.
The square is quietest early in the morning.

name: Rynek Underground
label: Rynek Underground
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1332080339: the OpenStreetMap point 'Rynek Underground'.
notes: Museum of medieval Kraków beneath the Main Square.

text.description:
Rynek Underground is a museum beneath Krakow's main market square, and it makes a very different photo stop from the busy square above. The space covers roughly 4,000 square metres. You walk along glass walkways over the remains of medieval constructions, and the main exhibition uses projections, fog and screens to suggest the city as it was about seven hundred years ago. That mix of dim light, glass and glowing projections gives you moody, atmospheric pictures.

The museum opened in September 2010. Among the displays are a reconstructed 12th-century workshop, the remains of old waterworks, traces of burned settlements from the eleventh century and a reconstructed merchant's stall. A huge medieval lump of lead, known as the "loaf" and weighing 693 kg, is also on show.

For your phone, the best pictures are usually the ones with a clear subject: a glass walkway leading away from you, a lit display case, or a projection with a few people in silhouette. Interiors like this are dark, so hold the phone steady with both hands and rest your elbows against your body. Wipe the lens before you go in, as glass and low light show up every smudge. Reflections in the glass can spoil a shot, so move a step to one side until they disappear. Check the museum's rules on photography before you start shooting, and be considerate of other visitors.
text.geographic_location: Directly beneath the main market square of Krakow, with parts of the exhibition underneath the Cloth Hall.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head to the market square on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the spot itself, so once you are on the market square you are in the right place. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the larger spaces to fit in the walkways and the displays. Use telephoto (2x or more) only for details in lit display cases.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a walkway so it leads into the picture. Keep the phone level so the glass floor and display edges stay straight. Include a person at a distance to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the brightest part, such as a projection or lit display, then lower the exposure slider a little so the glow keeps its detail. Use night mode only if you can hold very still, and avoid flash because it reflects off the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Inside, the light is the same all day, so pick a quieter time with fewer people in the frame. Early in the day is often calmer.

text.access_note: Check the museum's official information for entry details and photography rules before you go.

name: Cloth Hall
label: Cloth Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rynek Główny' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rynek Główny' (way/201133718): middle (416 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23256528: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cloth Hall' (141 m across).
notes: Renaissance trading hall in the middle of the Main Square.

text.description: The Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) is the long Renaissance building in the middle of Kraków's Main Market Square. It is one of the city's most recognisable monuments, and it photographs well because it sits in the centre of the square with open space on every side. Its arcades give you repeating arches, and from the southwest corner of the square St Mary's Basilica rises behind it with its two mismatched towers. In the 15th century this was a major centre of international trade. Merchants came here for spices, silk, leather and wax from the east, while Kraków sent out textiles, lead and salt from the Wieliczka Salt Mine. In the 19th century, under Austrian rule, the hall was renovated to a design by Tomasz Pryliński, and the Old Town around it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978. Upstairs is the Sukiennice Museum, with a large collection of 19th-century Polish painting and sculpture. For the classic full view, walk back to the southwest corner of the square, where the Cloth Hall fills the middle of the frame and the basilica towers sit above it. For a layered shot, step into the arcade and frame the basilica or the square between the arches. Another option is to stand near the monument in the square, which gives a cleaner picture with fewer café tables in view. Go early in the morning for fewer people. Dusk is also a good time, when the buildings are floodlit.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of the Main Market Square (Rynek Główny) in Kraków's Old Town. St Mary's Basilica rises behind the Cloth Hall when seen from the southwest corner of the square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town and the Main Market Square. The building is so large that you cannot miss it. For the full frame with the basilica towers, continue back to the southwest corner of the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long Cloth Hall into one frame at close range, and to include the basilica towers when you move back to the southwest corner. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers or a single run of arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rynek Główny (southwest corner of the square). The Cloth Hall in the middle of the frame with St Mary's Basilica's two mismatched towers rising behind it. At this distance the whole building will not fit comfortably in the middle of the frame, so use it for the arcades and details. For the full view with the two towers of St Mary's Basilica rising behind the hall, walk farther back to the southwest corner of the square. For a different angle, step into the arcade and shoot through the arches, or stand by the monument in the square for a cleaner view of the arcades.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the Cloth Hall's roofline level, then place the basilica towers just above it when you shoot from the southwest corner. Hold the phone steady and keep the vertical lines straight, because tilting it makes the buildings lean. When you shoot through the arcade, let the arches form a frame around the basilica or the square beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the building face to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the floodlit facades sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive. Dusk is also good, when the buildings are floodlit.

text.access_note: The square and the arcades are open public space, but the museum upstairs and the shops have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens helps fit the Cloth Hall, and from the southwest corner the basilica towers too, into one frame.
Keeping gridlines on helps keep the roofline level and the vertical lines straight.
Dragging the exposure slider down keeps the sky from washing out.
Night mode works best if the phone is braced against the body or a solid surface.
The stand-here point is too close (about 31 m) for the whole hall to fit comfortably in the middle of the frame, so the full view with the towers is taken from the farther southwest corner.

name: Old Synagogue
label: Old Synagogue
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ulica Szeroka' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of ulica Szeroka nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/152104775: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Synagogue' (39 m across).
notes: Oldest surviving synagogue in Poland, in Kazimierz.

text.description:
The Old Synagogue stands in the Kazimierz district of Kraków and is the oldest synagogue building still standing in Poland. It looks more like a small fortress than a place of prayer. The thick walls have heavy buttresses, and the attic wall has loopholes, features borrowed from military building. Dates given for when it was first built vary from 1407 to 1570, but it was rebuilt in 1570 by the Italian architect Mateo Gucci. Since 1958 it has been a branch of the Historical Museum of Kraków, focused on the city's Jewish history.

It photographs well because the north side is so varied. From further along ulica Szeroka you can see the arcaded roofline, the jagged outline of the women's gallery and the entrance vestibule in one frame. The street is open and gives you room to step back, which is what you need to fit the whole face of the building into a phone photo.

Start face east towards the synagogue and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean inwards. Switch on the gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal grid line. For the north-side view, move along the street until that side of the building comes into view and repeat the framing. If you have time, walk round to the small park on the east side. The eastern wall makes a quieter, more historical backdrop with paths and greenery beside it. Ulica Bartosza gives a third view, with the synagogue in the middle of the frame and older buildings behind.
text.geographic_location: In the Kazimierz district of Kraków, at 24 Szeroka Street, on the street's open frontage in front of the synagogue.
text.directions_text: No tram stop or station is listed for this spot, so head for Szeroka Street in the Kazimierz district, for example on foot or with a map app. From there the building lies 24 m to the east. Look for the long, buttressed walls and the arcaded roofline. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building from the street. If you can't step back far enough to fit the roofline and entrance, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the arcades or the jagged gallery roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on ulica Szeroka (from the street in front of the synagogue, facing its north side). The whole northern face of the synagogue, with its arcaded roofline, the jagged women's gallery and the entrance vestibule. To see the north side, with the arcaded roofline, the jagged women's gallery and the entrance vestibule, shift along the street until the whole northern face comes into view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone upright and level so the walls stay straight. Put the roofline on the upper grid line and leave some street at the bottom for scale. For a different view, try the eastern wall from the small park beside the building, or the view from ulica Bartosza, where the synagogue sits in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their colour and texture. At 0.5x, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually means softer light and fewer people in the frame, though the street is photogenic at any time of day.

text.access_note: The street and the outside of the building are public, but the museum inside may have its own visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: St. Florian's Gate
label: St. Florian's Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'ulica Pijarska' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of ulica Pijarska nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39357538: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Florian's Gate' (16 m across).
notes: Gothic gate of the medieval city walls.

text.description:
St. Florian's Gate is a tall, rectangular Gothic tower of rough stone, and it is the only one of Kraków's original eight medieval city gates that was not dismantled in the 19th century. It was first mentioned in 1307 and was part of the defences built after the Tatar attack of 1241. For centuries it was the main way into the Old Town, and the Royal Route to Wawel Castle starts here. The tower is 33.5 metres tall, with a Baroque metal helmet on top that dates from 1660 and adds about another metre. On the south face there is an 18th-century relief of St. Florian, and the north face carries a stone eagle carved in 1882 to a design by Jan Matejko.

It photographs well because the stonework is dark and textured and the outline is simple. The usual shot is straight down cobbled Floriańska Street, but that view is often crowded. This spot offers a calmer alternative: from ulica Pijarska, in the street north of the gate looking south, you see the whole tower with fewer people in the frame. Two other viewpoints are worth a look if you have time. One is Floriańska itself, with the gate closing the end of the street. The other is the Planty park, where the gate becomes an arch with the view running through towards St. Mary's Basilica.

Step back as far as the street allows so the top of the tower isn't cut off. Keep the phone upright and level so the walls don't lean. Short stretches of the old wall run alongside the gate, and they are used for street displays of art for sale.
text.geographic_location: St. Florian's Gate is at the northern edge of Kraków's Old Town, where Floriańska Street begins its run towards the Main Market Square. The side street ulica Pijarska passes beside it.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, train or tram stop at this spot, so start from the Old Town. From the Main Market Square, walk north up ulica Floriańska until the gate closes the end of the street. If you are coming from further out, walk in from the Old Town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole tower won't fit from where you stand. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the helmet or the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on ulica Pijarska (At the gap in the surviving wall fragments, where the side street runs past the gate). A side-on view of the full tower with few other people in the frame, showing the stonework lit from the east. At the gap in the surviving wall fragments where the side street runs past the gate. The photo shows the full tower, with few other people in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical edge of the tower up with one of them, so the walls stay straight. Leave a little sky above the helmet. A piece of the old wall in the foreground adds depth. For the classic street view, Floriańska shows the gate closing the end of the cobbled street. Planty frames the gate as an arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the bright sky doesn't wash out the detail. If a passer-by walks through, Live Photos can help you pick a clean frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is soft on the stonework.

text.access_note: The streets around the gate are open public space, but the gate's upper gallery and wall walk need a paid ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Kraków Barbican
label: Barbican
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Basztowa' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Basztowa nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13562708: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Barbican' (50 m across).
notes: Round brick fortress outside the Old Town walls.

text.description:
The Barbican is a round, moated brick fortress with seven little turrets, built around 1498 as an outpost in front of Kraków's city walls. It once linked to St. Florian's Gate by a covered passage and acted as a checkpoint for everyone entering the city. It is described as one of only three such fortified outposts still standing in Europe, and the best preserved. The walls are about 3 metres thick and hold 130 embrasures (narrow openings for defenders to shoot through). In 1817 two senators persuaded the city to keep it after it had been threatened with demolition.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear: a warm red-brown drum with a ring of turrets, set against paler townhouses and greenery. From Basztowa you see the whole fortress with the historic townhouses along the street framing it, which is the angle most people share. Keep the Barbican in the middle of the frame and let the buildings on either side lead the eye towards it. Because the fortress is quite compact, you can tilt the phone slightly up to keep the turrets sharp against the sky without cutting off the base.

If you have a few minutes, there are two other views. Standing by St. Florian's Gate (Brama Floriańska) frames the Barbican in the gateway, and the Planty park gives a fuller profile view of the turrets with trees around them.
text.geographic_location: The Barbican is at the Old Town's St. Florian's Gate in Kraków, where the old city walls once ran. Basztowa is the street beside it, lined with historic townhouses.
text.directions_text: Head for St. Florian's Gate on the edge of the Old Town, where the round fortress stands just outside the gate. Walk to the Old Town and on to St. Florian's Gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole round fortress and the townhouses beside it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the turrets or the moat edge are cut off, and use telephoto (2x or more) for close shots of the turrets and brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Basztowa. The round brick barbican with its turrets and defensive walls, framed by the historic townhouses along the street. From here you see the round brick fortress with its turrets and defensive walls, framed by the old townhouses along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the Barbican just off-centre, with the townhouses forming a line down one side. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a different view, try St. Florian's Gate (Brama Floriańska), which frames the Barbican in the gateway, or the Planty park for a fuller profile of the turrets with trees around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the brick keeps its colour. Wait a moment for passers-by to clear before you take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer light in the early morning or late afternoon usually flatters the brick and means fewer people in the frame. The outside views work all year.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public street; the inside is run as a museum site, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and flatters brick, and crowds are usually smaller then.
The Barbican may not fit fully into the frame at 1x from the stand-here point, so ultra-wide (0.5x) may help.
Passers-by on Basztowa may walk through the frame.

name: Ghetto Heroes Square
label: Ghetto Heroes Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac Bohaterów Getta' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4097302: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Plac Bohaterów Getta' (108 m across).
notes: Memorial square with empty bronze chairs.

text.description: Ghetto Heroes Square is a wide, paved square in Podgórze, and the memorial in it is what draws the camera. Seventy oversized metal chairs stand in a grid, all facing the same way. Seen across the square, that order looks quiet and deliberate, and the plain grey paving and the ordinary city behind the chairs make them stand out. The square was once called Mały Rynek, meaning Small Market Square. Between 1941 and 1943 it lay inside the Kraków Ghetto and was a gathering point for Jewish residents before deportation. The memorial was unveiled after the square was redeveloped in 2005. Its designers, Piotr Lewicki and Kazimierz Łatak, took their idea from Tadeusz Pankiewicz's account of furniture being carried out into the square as the houses were cleared. For photos, step in among the chairs and shoot across the paved square to show the whole grid. Then try a few different angles to see how the chairs stand against the buildings behind. Other good frames are rows of chairs in the foreground with the small historic police box behind, and the chairs along the eastern edge with the tram stop canopy in view, which puts the memorial next to everyday street life. This is a place of remembrance, so keep your photos respectful and avoid pointing the phone at other visitors.
text.geographic_location: In the Podgórze district of Krakow, in the open square once known as Mały Rynek and now called Plac Bohaterów Getta. The memorial chairs fill much of the square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Podgórze district and ask for Plac Bohaterów Getta. Once you are in the square, walk in among the chairs to reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the chair grid. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole square in one frame. Use 2x if your phone has it to pull a few rows of chairs together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You get a wide frame of the grey paving with the large metal chairs in their grid and the surrounding city behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the rows of chairs with them so the layout looks tidy. Crouch a little to bring the chairs closer to the lens and make them look larger against the backdrop. For a second picture, put rows of chairs in the foreground with the small police box behind them. Another option is to go to the eastern edge, where the tram stop canopy shows the memorial beside normal street life.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a chair to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the grey paving keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out. Keep the ultra-wide close to the chairs, because it stretches things at the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: This is an open public square with a memorial, so no ticket is needed. Please be respectful, and check the official site before you go for any events or changes.

name: Kościuszko Mound
label: Kościuszko Mound
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Błonia' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Błonia' (relation/14476568): edge nearest the subject (2628 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Kościuszko's Mound'.
notes: Hilltop mound with a panorama over the city.

text.description:
Kościuszko Mound (Kopiec Kościuszki) is a large artificial hill in the western part of Kraków's Zwierzyniec District. Cracovians raised it in memory of the Polish national leader Tadeusz Kościuszko, and it was finished in November 1823. People of all ages and classes helped to build it, and it stands about 35 metres high. It was modelled on Kraków's ancient mounds of Krak and Wanda. In the 1850s the Austrian authorities built a brick citadel around it, and a neo-Gothic chapel of Blessed Bronisława belongs to the same story.

From here the mound rises above the grass, and the Old Town towers appear in the same view. That combination of wide green space, a smooth dome-shaped hill and the city skyline is what makes the picture work. The mound is a good distance away, so it will look small if you only shoot at the default lens (1x). Zoom in to bring it closer, and keep some of the meadow in the frame to give a sense of scale.

If you want a second angle, Las Wolski offers a more distant view of Wawel Castle and the mound, framed by the green of the forest. Going up the mound itself is a different kind of visit, with its panoramic views over the city and the Vistula. Check the official site before you go if you plan to climb it.
text.geographic_location: The mound stands on Blessed Bronisława Hill in the western part of Kraków's Zwierzyniec District.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot. From there the mound lies to the south-west, about 1.1 km away. If you want to visit the mound itself, keep walking in that direction. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the mound and the Old Town towers closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the meadow and sky better than the mound, which will look very small at that setting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Błonia (the meadow below the mound, on the mound's lower side). The mound rising above the open meadow, with the Old Town towers visible in the same view. The broad meadow below the mound, on the mound's lower side. From here the mound rises above the grass, and the Old Town towers appear in the same view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the mound on one of the upper lines, with the meadow filling the lower third. Try to keep the Old Town towers in the frame so the photo says 'Kraków'. Crouching a little lowers the horizon and makes the mound look taller. For a different view, Las Wolski gives a distant shot of Wawel Castle and the mound framed by the forest.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mound to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the hill keeps its colour and the sky doesn't turn white. At 3x or more, hold the phone steady with both hands, and rest your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and try the early morning or the hour before sunset, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: Błonia is a broad meadow, but the mound itself is a visitor site, so check the official site before you go if you want to climb it.
claims_not_in_sources: A clear day with soft light in the early morning or just before sunset usually suits this view best.
The mound looks small at the default lens (1x) from this distance, so zooming helps.

name: Town Hall Tower
label: Town Hall Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rynek Główny' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rynek Główny' (way/201133718): middle (416 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25122842: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Town Hall Tower' (23 m across).
notes: Lone Gothic tower left from the old town hall.

text.description:
Town Hall Tower is the one piece left of Kraków's old Town Hall, which was pulled down in 1820 to open up the Main Market Square. It was built at the end of the 14th century in stone and brick and stands 70 metres tall. A storm in 1703 left it leaning by just 55 centimetres. That slight tilt is what makes it a good subject: against the Old Town rooftops it looks a little less stiff than a perfectly upright tower.

The tower photographs best as a whole, rising over the square with open space around its base. Look for the pair of stone lions guarding the entrance, and the Gothic portal above the door with the city coat of arms. They make a good detail shot once you are close.

One guide loosely suggests the south side of the square, because the lean shows well from there. Keep the whole tower in the frame, with a little rooftop and sky around it, and turn on gridlines so you can judge the upright lines against the tilt. If you want a second picture, step slightly to the side of the Cloth Hall arcades so the tower stands clear beside them. Another option is ulica Bracka, where the tower is framed at the end of the street.

The top floor has an observation deck, but that is an indoor, ticketed view and not part of this ground-level shot.
text.geographic_location: A focal point of the Main Market Square (Rynek Główny) in Kraków's Old Town, near the Cloth Hall.
text.directions_text: Head to the Old Town and the Main Market Square (Rynek Główny), where the tower stands in the open. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole tower fits with some rooftops around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the lions and doorway close up. If your phone has a 2x-3x telephoto, use it for a tighter shot of the upper part of the tower without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rynek Główny (south side of the square, looking north-northwest at the tower). The tower rising over the square with its slight lean visible, framed against the Old Town rooftops. From here it rises over the square with its slight lean visible, framed against the Old Town rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line, so the lean is easy to see. Leave a little sky above the top. For a different view, step slightly to the side of the Cloth Hall arcades so the tower stands fully clear beside them, or try ulica Bracka, where the tower is framed at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone level so the tower doesn't look as if it leans further than it does.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually calmer, with fewer people crossing your frame. Soft daylight suits the stonework.

text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the open public square; for the observation deck and any museum entry, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the square is usually calmer, with fewer people crossing the frame.
Soft daylight suits the stonework of the tower.
Gridlines help show the tower's slight lean against a vertical line.

name: Collegium Maius
label: Collegium Maius
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jagiellońska' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Jagiellońska and Świętej Anny (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/214263: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Collegium Maius' (101 m across).
notes: Oldest building of the Jagiellonian University, with an arcaded courtyard.

text.description:
Collegium Maius is the oldest building of the Jagiellonian University, with parts dating back to the 14th century. It stands in Kraków's Old Town, close to the Main Square, at the corner of ulica Jagiellońska and ulica Świętej Anny. The university moved in after King Władysław II Jagiełło bought the building with money left by his late wife, Queen Jadwiga. It was rebuilt in the late 15th century in late-Gothic style around a large arcaded courtyard, and a well was added in the middle in 1517. Nicolaus Copernicus was among its students in the 1490s. Today it houses the Jagiellonian University Museum.

It photographs well because there are two quite different pictures here. From the street corner you can frame the oldest stone-built part of the college, with its Gothic gable and bay window, and the street is usually calmer than the courtyard. Inside, the brick arcades around the well and the courtyard clock make a more classic shot. Both are worth a few frames if you have time.

On a phone, the corner suits a tall, careful composition, so keep the gable and bay window as the main subject and let the street fill the lower part of the picture. If the courtyard is open to you, use its arcades as a frame. Photography rules inside the museum rooms may differ from the courtyard, so check before you take pictures indoors.
text.geographic_location: In Kraków's Old Town, a short walk from the Main Square, at the corner of ulica Jagiellońska and ulica Świętej Anny.
text.directions_text: Start from the Main Square (Rynek Główny) and head to the corner of ulica Jagiellońska and ulica Świętej Anny, which is close by. If you are coming from further out, head to the Main Square area and walk the rest. Once you are the main part of the building is to the west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the corner, because you may be standing close to the building and it helps fit the whole gable and bay window in. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the details of the gable and bay window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Jagiellońska and Świętej Anny (corner of the building, at the oldest part of the college). The oldest, stone-built part of the college at the corner of the two streets, with its Gothic gable and bay window in view. From here the oldest stone-built part of the college is in view, with its Gothic gable and bay window. Face west towards the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edge of the building with a vertical line so the walls do not lean. Keep the gable and bay window as the main subject, with a little street at the bottom for scale. For a second view, go into the courtyard and shoot the Gothic brick arcades around the central well, with the courtyard clock on one side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stone to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky and pale stonework keep their detail. In the courtyard, try a Live Photo around the clock, and check the clock times locally before you go as they may vary.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning or on a softer, overcast day for the quietest street and the gentlest light on the stone. The courtyard is likely to be busier around the middle of the day.

text.access_note: The street corner is in the open public street, but access to the courtyard and museum rooms, and the photography rules inside, may differ, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The street corner is usually quieter than the courtyard.
Early morning or overcast days give softer light and fewer people, and the courtyard may be busier around midday.
The courtyard clock may run on a set schedule, but the times vary between listings, so they should be checked locally.
Access to the courtyard and museum rooms, and photography rules inside, may differ from the street.

name: Floriańska Street
label: Floriańska Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brama Floriańska' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Brama Floriańska' (way/39357538): middle (16 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3989492: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Floriańska' (346 m long).
notes: Busy Old Town street leading from St. Florian's Gate to the Main Square.

text.description:
Floriańska Street is one of the best-known walks in Kraków's Old Town. It runs in a dead-straight line from the north-east corner of the Main Market Square to St. Florian's Gate, about 335 metres in all. It appears on the 1257 plan of the extended city, was part of the Royal Road, and is named after Saint Florian. A horse tram ran along it from 1882. Today the tall town houses on either side hold shops, cafés and restaurants. Among them are the Jan Matejko House and the Jama Michalika café.

The street photographs well because it is so straight. The gate arch makes a dark frame, and the tower of St. Mary's Basilica sits at the far end. Guides often call this the signature view of the street, and it has appeared in paintings and postcards for a long time. Stand just inside the arch on the gate's inner side and look south-west down the street. Let the arch edges sit around the picture, and keep the basilica near the middle so the street leads the eye to it.

It is a pedestrian street and is usually crowded, so early morning is the common advice. Wait for a gap between groups, take several shots, and pick the one with the cleanest foreground. For a second angle, try photographing the gate itself from the church end.
text.geographic_location: Floriańska Street is in Kraków Old Town. It links the north-east corner of the Main Market Square with St. Florian's Gate in the line of the old defensive walls.
text.directions_text: From the Main Market Square, walk along Floriańska Street to St. Florian's Gate at the north-east end. The street is about 335 metres long. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight view down the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole arch around the picture in a tight spot. Try the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the basilica at the far end closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Brama Floriańska (under the arch on the gate's inner (south) side, looking down the street). The straight run of Floriańska Street framed by the gate arch, with St. Mary's Basilica visible at the far end. From here the photo shows the straight run of Floriańska Street framed by the arch, with St. Mary's Basilica at the far end. The street runs away from you to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the street's centre with the middle of the frame, keeping your phone level so the buildings stand straight. Let the arch edges frame the picture, and keep the basilica near the centre. For another view, try Plac Mariacki, with the street running away from the basilica towards the gate. Alternatively, you could try a view reminiscent of the historic painting known as Zacisze, from some distance away; check the position on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the far end of the street, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and buildings keep their detail. Take a few frames in a row, as people keep moving through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the usual advice, as the street is a busy pedestrian route for much of the day.

text.access_note: Floriańska Street is an open pedestrian street, and standing under the gate arch is free. The gate's upper parts and interior are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Church of Saints Peter and Paul
label: Saints Peter and Paul
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Plac św. Marii Magdaleny' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Plac Świętej Marii Magdaleny' (way/25128175): middle (57 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/104374972: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Saints Peter and Paul' (77 m across).
notes: Baroque church on Grodzka Street with apostle statues in front.

text.description: The Church of Saints Peter and Paul is a Baroque church on Grodzka Street in Kraków's Old Town. It was built between 1597 and 1619 and paid for by King Sigismund III Vasa for the Jesuits. It is described as the first building in Kraków designed entirely in the Baroque style, and it is the biggest of the city's historic churches by seating capacity. It photographs well because the facade is tall, pale and richly detailed. Statues of Jesuit saints stand in its niches, and the Vasa coat of arms sits at the very top. In front, a limestone fence carries a row of apostle sculptures. These are modern copies, made to replace 18th-century originals that acid rain badly damaged. Marii Magdaleny. From there the facade and tower are seen straight on across the square, with the Piotr Skarga monument in the foreground. Skarga, a Jesuit preacher, is buried in the church. The square is small and usually busy, so an early or off-peak visit gives you a clearer frame. If you want a different angle, walk to Grodzka street for a lower frame with the fence and apostle sculptures leading up to the front.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Kraków, on Grodzka Street (number 52a). The best viewing square, Plac św. Marii Magdaleny, sits across from the church facade.
text.directions_text: The church is on Grodzka street in the Old Town, so head for Grodzka street. From Plac św. Look for the limestone fence with the row of apostle sculptures in front of the facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the facade and tower. If the square is too crowded to step back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit it all in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues in the niches and the coat of arms at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Plac św. Marii Magdaleny (open side facing Grodzka street, across from the church facade). The baroque facade and tower of the church seen straight on across the small square, with the Piotr Skarga monument in the foreground. Stand on Plac św. Marii Magdaleny, on the open side facing Grodzka street, across from the church facade. The church is to the east of you. From here you see the baroque facade and tower straight on across the small square, with the Piotr Skarga monument in the foreground. This is the classic postcard angle and also shows the neighbouring St Andrew's church beside the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical grid line so the facade does not lean. Use the Skarga monument as a foreground anchor at one edge of the frame. For a second shot, walk to Grodzka street and shoot low along the limestone fence, so the apostle sculptures lead your eye up to the front of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as passers-by often walk through the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early or at an off-peak time, when the small square is less busy with tourists.

text.access_note: The exterior views from the square and Grodzka street are in open public space, but the church is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
